planting.note: Root stem cuttings or offsets in spring in lean, gritty succulent mix in bright light; this subshrub branches and develops a short trunk with age, so give it room and a sturdy container.

directions: Unlike most stemless rosette succulents in this group, this species develops a visible branching stem over time, carrying clusters of thick, pale green to blue-gray leaves at each tip. It tolerates more heat and sun than many soft succulents once established, and stems can be air-layered or cut back to control its spreading habit. Grow in sharply drained, mineral-rich soil and let it dry fully between waterings, since the fleshy stems and leaves are prone to rot in damp conditions. Older plants benefit from an occasional hard pruning to encourage denser, more compact branching.

planting.note: Divide trailing offsets or root detached rosettes in spring in shallow, gritty soil in full sun; the low, spreading habit makes it well suited to wide pans or hanging containers.

directions: This low, mat-forming species spreads outward on short trailing stems, each tipped with a small rosette of thick, bluish-gray leaves. It stays close to the soil surface rather than forming a single tall rosette, making it a good choice for edging gritty succulent beds or spilling over the rim of a shallow bowl. Grow in full sun with very sharp drainage, watering thoroughly and then letting the mix dry out completely before watering again. New rosettes root readily where stems touch soil, making it easy to expand plantings from a single start.

planting.note: Divide offset clusters in spring and plant shallowly in fast-draining soil in full sun to light shade; its small scale suits troughs, dish gardens, and rock crevices.

directions: Native to the mountains of Sonora, Chihuahua, and Durango, this is one of the smallest species in its genus, forming tight, compact rosettes of thick, pale blue-gray to pale green leaves that often blush pink under strong sun. Its naturally cold-tolerant high-elevation origin makes it somewhat more cold-hardy in cultivation than many lowland relatives, though it still needs protection from hard freezes. Plant in very lean, mineral soil and water sparingly, allowing the mix to dry completely between waterings. It offsets readily into dense little colonies, making division the easiest way to propagate established clumps.

planting.note: Divide dense rosette clusters in spring and set shallowly in gritty, well-drained soil in bright light; frequent light watering in active growth keeps the small rosettes plump.

directions: This small Mexican species forms dense mats of tiny, tightly packed rosettes with thick, pale green leaves that can flush reddish under bright light and dry conditions. Its compact, carpeting habit suits shallow pans, crevice gardens, and mixed succulent bowls where its low profile contrasts with taller rosette succulents. It appreciates a bit more regular summer moisture than many of its genus relatives but still needs sharply draining, mineral-rich soil to prevent rot. Clumps spread steadily by offsetting and are simplest to propagate by dividing rooted sections.

planting.note: Root offsets or leaf cuttings in spring in gritty, well-drained succulent mix in full sun; cool nights and bright light intensify the ruffled pink leaf margins.

directions: Native to Mexico, this species forms a modest rosette of grayish-green leaves with gently ruffled, pink-flushed margins that deepen in color under strong light and cool weather. Tall, slender flowering stalks rise above the foliage, carrying nodding, bell-shaped blooms favored by hummingbirds. It offsets readily around the base, producing small plantlets that can be detached once they have their own roots. Grow in sharply draining soil in full sun, watering deeply and then letting the mix dry out completely before watering again to avoid rot in the rosette center.

common_name: Glowing Echeveria (Desert Rosette with Coral Flowers)

planting.note: Plant offsets or rooted leaf cuttings in spring in lean, mineral soil in full sun to light shade; this dry-shrubland native tolerates heat and drought better than many soft-leaved relatives.

directions: Found growing wild across dry shrublands in central Mexico, this compact rosette species produces fleshy, often blue-green leaves that can take on warm coppery tones under intense sun. Short flowering stalks emerge from the center of the rosette bearing clusters of glowing coral to orange blooms that attract pollinators through much of the growing season. It handles brief cold better than many tender echeverias but still needs protection from hard freezes and standing winter moisture. Plant in very fast-draining soil and allow it to dry out fully between waterings.

planting.note: Root offsets or leaf cuttings in spring in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; keep water out of the rosette center and remove spent lower leaves as the plant matures.

directions: This Mexican species forms a substantial rosette of broad, soft green leaves whose edges are crinkled and finely rippled, taking on reddish to brown tones along the margins in bright light. Clusters of pinkish to yellow, bell-shaped flowers rise on arching stalks above the foliage during the growing season. As the plant matures it tends to shed its lower leaves, leaving a short bare stem beneath the rosette that is best left in place rather than trimmed. Grow in full sun with sharply draining soil, watering thoroughly and then letting the mix dry out completely to prevent rot.

planting.note: Root offsets or stem cuttings in spring in lean, gritty soil in full sun; this larger-growing species benefits from a sturdy pot or bed as it ages.

directions: Unusual among echeverias for its native range in the high-elevation shrublands of Peru rather than Mexico, this species develops a sizable rosette of fleshy, succulent leaves on a short, often visible stem as it matures. Clusters of flowers rise from the rosette center on short stalks typical of the genus, drawing pollinators during the warm growing months. It tolerates intense sun and heat well but still requires sharply draining, mineral soil and should be kept dry through winter. Propagate by rooting offsets or firm stem cuttings rather than relying on seed.

common_name: Fringed Echeveria (Burgundy Rosette with Hair-Edged Leaves)

planting.note: Root offsets or leaf cuttings in spring in gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun; cool nights and bright light bring out the deepest burgundy leaf color.

directions: This vigorous, fast-growing species forms rosettes of broad, oval leaves that shift from green to deep maroon under strong light and cool temperatures, with fine hair-like fringing along the leaf edges that gives the species its name. It grows and offsets more quickly than many slower echeverias, making it a satisfying choice for building up container groupings. Plant in sharply draining, mineral-rich soil in full sun and water thoroughly, then let the soil dry out completely before the next watering. Propagate new plants from offsets or individual leaves pressed lightly into gritty rooting medium.
